sections.heading: Title
sections.text: Mixture models usually blend simple distributions by adding them together. But what if a mixture could also subtract probability mass? This paper, published at ICLR 2024, shows how to learn deep subtractive mixtures by squaring them. The trick keeps the model a valid probability distribution while allowing negative parameters, and the authors prove these squared non-monotonic circuits can be exponentially more compact than ordinary additive mixtures, then confirm the gain on real-world density estimation and on distilling a language model.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.text: Traditional mixture models build complex distributions by blending simple ones in a convex, additive combination. That works, but it can be wildly inefficient. If the distribution you want has gaps or holes in its domain, an additive mixture has to stack up many components just to carve those holes out. The natural fix is to let some components subtract probability mass instead of only adding it. The catch is that once you allow subtraction, the model can dip below zero and stop being a valid probability distribution, and learning it becomes genuinely hard.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.text: So why revisit this now? Because subtraction pays off dramatically: a mixture that can cancel mass can capture complex shapes with far fewer components. The problem is guaranteeing the result stays non-negative. Energy-based models handle non-negativity by exponentiation, but then you lose the ability to normalize the model tractably. Meanwhile, several separate research communities, from signal processing to kernel methods to quantum mechanics, each rediscovered a squaring trick to enforce non-negativity, but without a common, tractable framework tying them together.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.text: This work makes four contributions. First, it introduces a general framework for representing subtractive mixtures by squaring, expressed in the language of tensorized probabilistic circuits. Second, it shows these squared non-monotonic circuits generalize several apparently different models that allow negative parameters, including square-root-of-density models, positive semi-definite kernel models, and Born machines from quantum physics. Third, it proves an exponential lower bound: there are functions a single squared circuit encodes compactly that any monotonic circuit needs exponentially more units to represent. And fourth, it backs all of this with experiments on real-world data.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Here is the core idea. Take a mixture with unconstrained real weights, so components can have negative coefficients, and simply square the whole thing. Squaring forces the output to be non-negative no matter what the weights are. Expanding the square turns a K-component mixture into a sum over all pairs of components, a product of experts form, where the partition function that renormalizes it can still be computed in closed form for many families. To go deep, the authors square a tensorized structured-decomposable circuit layer by layer. Each squared layer holds a quadratic number of units but still outputs a vector, so the whole model trains efficiently with gradient descent, computing the normalizer just once per batch.

sections.heading: Dataset / Benchmark
sections.text: The experiments cover three regimes. First, two-dimensional synthetic densities, both continuous and discrete, where you can literally see how well each model captures rings and other holey shapes. Second, five standard UCI multivariate datasets: Power, Gas, Hepmass, MiniBooNE, and BSDS300. And third, a language-model distillation task, where the models are trained to approximate sentences sampled from GPT2. Baselines span full-covariance Gaussians, modern normalizing flows like RealNVP, MADE, MAF and NSF, monotonic probabilistic circuits, and tensor-train density estimators.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.text: The headline finding is consistent: at the same model size, squared non-monotonic circuits reach higher log-likelihoods than monotonic circuits across the density estimation tasks. On the two-dimensional ring distributions, you can see that plain squaring already helps, but it is the negative parameters that let the model actually carve out the holes in the density. And on the GPT2 distillation task, the squared circuits scale better and get closer to GPT2's own likelihood, meaning they approximate the intractable language model more faithfully than monotonic circuits do.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.text: To be sure the gains come from subtraction and not just from squaring, the authors compare against squared monotonic circuits, which square but keep all parameters non-negative. The squared non-monotonic circuits still win, confirming that the negative parameters are doing the real work. Two other patterns emerge: binary-tree region graphs generally beat linear-tree ones, and the choice of input layer matters, with splines helping most on continuous data and embeddings helping on discrete data. On some discrete image-mass tasks, where the inputs are already expressive, the advantage narrows.

sections.heading: Headline Numbers
sections.text: A few numbers make the point. Squaring a mixture with K components encodes on the order of K squared over two pairwise components while reusing the same K parameters, which is where the compactness comes from, and the paper proves this compactness gap over monotonic circuits is exponential. Empirically, the squared non-monotonic circuits post the best test log-likelihoods among tractable models on several UCI datasets, for example zero point six two on Power, about eleven on Gas, minus twenty point four on Hepmass, and minus twenty-six point seven on MiniBooNE. On the language data, they climb toward GPT2's own likelihood of around minus fifty-two while monotonic circuits flatten out.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.text: The takeaway is simple. Squaring turns subtractive mixtures into valid, tractable probabilistic models that need exponentially fewer components than additive mixtures to reach the same expressiveness. Along the way, this single framework unifies square-root-of-density models, positive semi-definite kernel models, and quantum Born machines under one property-driven view of circuits. The result makes subtraction a practical, first-class tool for building compact and expressive probabilistic models.
